statement: In healthy adults in crossover studies, mostly in sleep laboratories, caffeine taken earlier in the day, compared with no caffeine or placebo, reduces that night's sleep: about 45 minutes less total sleep (95% CI 29 to 62), about 9 minutes longer to fall asleep (3.8 to 14.4), about 12 minutes more waking during the night (2.5 to 21.0), 7 percentage points lower sleep efficiency (4 to 10) and a shift from deep to light sleep, in a meta-analysis of 24 studies (Gardiner et al., 2023). statement: In adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician and tested in laboratories while off psychiatric medicines, a single oral caffeine challenge (480 mg printed in 7 of 10 studies; the caffeine-equivalent amount of one citrate-labelled protocol is unclear; study conditions), compared with placebo in within-person study designs, increases the chance of a panic attack within hours, by a meta-analysis of 10 small blinded challenge studies published from 1985 to 2015 (Klevebrant & Frick, 2022): in the 9 studies that reported panic attacks, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51 in 100) had one after caffeine, and no study reported one after placebo; in the 6 studies that also tested people without panic disorder, 69 of 128 people with panic disorder (54 in 100) had one after caffeine against 2 of 115 healthy controls (2 in 100), a difference of 52 in 100 (editors' calculation). The paper prints two incompatible pooled risk ratios for that comparison (about 32 by its text and 12.1 in its figure), so the counts are the better summary. Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more on average in people with panic disorder (standardized difference 1.02, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.96), but the studies varied widely (prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 without one outlying study, editors' recalculation), and these pooled rises were changes after caffeine rather than a pooled caffeine-versus-placebo contrast. Separately, the review reports that all five studies making a statistical caffeine-versus-placebo anxiety comparison found a greater rise after caffeine; usable placebo change data were inconsistently described and too sparse to pool. The study protocols do not establish a dose-response relationship or the effects of ordinary smaller servings. Table 1 labels one weight-based preparation caffeine citrate without clarifying whether its amount refers to caffeine or the salt; neither a corrected caffeine-equivalent amount nor an exact lower tested boundary is established here. One participant received caffeine only, so the caffeine denominator is not a verified complete paired-placebo denominator. All studies were done at rest during a break from psychiatric medicines; 2 always gave caffeine last, and 8 of the 10 come from two research groups. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small laboratory studies, about half of adults with panic disorder had a panic attack after a caffeine challenge (121 of 237). None was reported after a dummy drink or capsule, though not everyone completed both conditions. Among people without panic disorder, 2 of 115 had an attack after caffeine. Most studies used one large amount. The review does not show what ordinary smaller servings do, and one study's caffeine amount is unclear. Anxiety also rose more after caffeine than after a dummy in all five studies that tested that comparison.
population: Adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician (DSM-III to DSM-5 or ICD criteria), mostly recruited from outpatient clinics and tested during a break from psychiatric medicines: 244 people in 10 studies (1985 to 2015), and 122 psychiatrically healthy controls in 7 of the studies
exposure: Single oral caffeine challenge protocols at rest: 480 mg printed in seven studies and 400 mg in one; two protocols printed 7 mg/kg and caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg. The review converts the weight-based protocols at 75 kg, but does not clarify whether the citrate-labelled amount is caffeine or salt. No corrected caffeine-equivalent range is inferred. Capsules, instant coffee or other drinks (study conditions only).
comparator: Placebo of the same or similar taste in within-person study designs; one Tancer participant received caffeine only. Healthy controls given the same challenge in seven studies.
outcome: Panic attack within 30 to 240 minutes (self- or clinician-reported); change in self-rated anxiety
magnitude: Klevebrant & Frick (2022): panic attacks after caffeine 121/237 (51.1%) with panic disorder in 9 studies and 2/115 (1.7%) controls; none after placebo in any study. In the 6 studies with both groups 69/128 (53.9%) against 2/115 (1.7%), risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation); pooled log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) in the text, which is RR about 32 (7.8 to 130; editors' calculation), against RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) in Fig. 4. Studies without controls: 52/109 (47.7%). Anxiety change after caffeine (6 studies; 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36); difference g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), I² 66.8%, prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37) without the outlying study (editors' recalculation). Oral protocols mostly print 480 mg; the citrate-labelled protocol's caffeine-equivalent dose basis is unresolved. All five studies testing caffeine versus placebo statistically reported greater anxiety after caffeine; the pooled anxiety changes did not compare against placebo.

risk_of_bias.note: Two of the ten studies always gave caffeine last; outcome-assessor blinding unclear in most (approximate reading of the review's figure); per-study judgments not read. The review itself is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_klevebrant_2022): two incompatible pooled risk ratios, an inconsistently described model, risk of bias never discussed, English-language published reports only.

inconsistency.note: All six studies with both groups point the same way, and about half of the people with panic disorder had an attack in the studies with and without controls (54 and 48 in 100); the anxiety results vary more but are described, not graded.

indirectness.note: Second-hand primary evidence (METHODS §6.3) from selected acute oral protocols, mostly 480 mg as printed, at rest in a laboratory; the citrate-labelled protocol has an unresolved dose basis, during a break from psychiatric medicines; everyday intake, people on treatment and life outside the laboratory were not studied.

imprecision.note: The proportions rest on 237 people with panic disorder and 115 controls and agree across studies; the unstable pooled ratio is not used.

publication_bias.note: No small-study effect was seen for panic attacks; with six studies no test is possible, and the search excluded unpublished and non-English reports. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Blinded placebo-controlled within-person challenge studies start high; rated down for risk of bias (two fixed-order studies, assessor blinding mostly unclear, and a review whose pooled ratios disagree) and indirectness (single large doses at rest in a laboratory, off medication): low. 'Increases' rests on the within-person comparison with placebo: about half had a panic attack after caffeine and none after placebo. The comparison with healthy controls is not randomized and is shown as counts, not as a ratio. The pooled anxiety results are described, not graded: changes after caffeine rather than a pooled placebo contrast, with a prediction interval including no group difference. Separately, all five statistical caffeine-versus-placebo anxiety comparisons favoured greater anxiety after caffeine. The primary evidence is second-hand; that indirectness shares the existing domain downgrade with applicability limits. One caffeine-only participant prevents assuming a complete 237-person paired placebo denominator. The primary studies were not read; the counts are the review's text and Table 1. Status replicated: 9 studies from at least two independent research groups point the same way, though studies within each group are not independent of each other.

statement: In 50 healthy non-smoking men aged 18 to 46 at the University of Birmingham, UK, who habitually drank 3 to 6 cups of coffee a day (300 to 600 mg of caffeine a day by a 3-day weighed food diary), drinking four 200 mL mugs of black instant coffee a day for 3 days (study conditions: 4 mg of caffeine per kg of body weight a day by design; mean 308 mg, range 204.4 to 453.0 mg) compared with four 200 mL mugs of water a day, in a randomized, counterbalanced crossover with all food and each man's daily bottled water prescribed from his food diary and identical in both trials (whether the test drinks counted within that water is not stated), does not detectably change daily urine output or the other hydration markers measured: 24-hour urine volume averaged 2,409 mL (2.41 litres) a day with coffee and 2,428 mL (2.43 litres) with water (± 660 and 669, unlabelled, read as SDs); urine specific gravity was 1.009 in all four 24-hour collections; and urine osmolality and creatinine, morning urine volume and specific gravity, fasting blood markers (haematocrit, serum osmolality, sodium, potassium, total protein, creatinine and urea) and morning body weight did not differ between the trials (only urine volume, urine specific gravity and body weight are reported for all 50 men; the other markers here for 42 to 49 each, or without a number). Body weight fell slightly within both trials (0.39 kg from day 1 to day 3 across both, about 0.5% of body weight by the editors' calculation, against the 1% to 3% loss the authors cite as clinical dehydration). The one difference was urinary sodium, higher with coffee in both 24-hour collections (48.7 against 43.6 and 47.0 against 43.4 mmol, p = 0.02). Total body water by deuterium dilution, which the authors call the gold standard, did not change significantly in either trial (Figure 2 shows numerical rises in both) and did not differ between the trials (51.5 ± 1.4 against 51.4 ± 1.3 kg, the ± not labelled), but it is shown for only 25 of the 50 men, with no reason given, and its ± values look like standard errors rather than SDs (editors' reading). 'Similar' rests on differences that were not statistically significant: the paper reports no confidence interval, no power calculation and no within-person differences. By the editors' calculation from the printed means and ± values (read as SDs), treating the two trials as independent groups (which can only widen the interval when a man's two trials are positively correlated), the urine difference of −19 mL a day has a 95% interval of about −290 to +250 mL a day: an effect as large as the 41% rise in urine that the authors cite from an earlier study of six cups after 5 days without caffeine (about 1 litre a day on these men's output, editors' arithmetic) would have been detectable, but a coffee excess of up to about a quarter of a litre of urine a day cannot be excluded. For these men the water trial meant 3 days without coffee, and withdrawal was not measured; there was no decaffeinated-coffee arm, and urine was not measured in the hours after each cup. Funded by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee, described in the paper as a non-profit organisation devoted to science on coffee and health, with no role in the study; one author was employed by PepsiCo (Killer et al., 2014). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 3-day test in Birmingham, UK, 50 healthy men who already drank coffee every day had black instant coffee on some days and the same amount of water on others, with their food and other drinks kept the same. They peed about the same amount: 2.41 litres a day on coffee days and 2.43 litres on water days. Urine strength, blood tests and body weight did not differ either; the only difference was a little more salt in the urine on coffee days. Body water was measured too, but results were shown for only 25 of the men. The study reported no ranges and no power calculation, so it could have missed a small effect, and it says nothing about women, people who rarely have caffeine or larger amounts. A coffee research institute paid for it.
population: 50 healthy non-smoking men aged 18 to 46 (mean 28.1, SD 7.3; weight 77.0 kg, SD 12.1) who habitually drank 3 to 6 cups of coffee a day (300 to 600 mg of caffeine a day by a 3-day weighed food diary; habitual coffee 979 mL a day, SD 301), accepted after screening of over 100 volunteers at the University of Birmingham, UK, and tested Tuesday to Friday between February and December (year not given); 52 enrolled and 50 completed both trials; women were excluded
exposure: Four 200 mL mugs a day of black instant coffee (Nescafé Original, 2.3 ± 0.4 g per cup, ± unlabelled) made with boiled tap water, at fixed times on 3 consecutive trial days after a control day (study conditions: 4 mg of caffeine per kg of body weight a day by design; mean 308 mg a day, range 204.4 to 453.0 mg), with all food and each man's daily bottled water (mean 1953 ± 642 mL a day, ± unlabelled; set from his food diary; whether the test drinks counted within it is not stated) prescribed individually, provided and identical in both trials; alcohol and exercise other than walking not allowed
comparator: Four 200 mL mugs of tap water a day in the same men in the other trial (random allocation to a counterbalanced order, 10-day washout on their usual diet and caffeine); day-2 serum caffeine was lower than in the coffee trial (p<0.01); no decaffeinated-coffee arm
outcome: 24-hour urine volume, specific gravity, osmolality, creatinine, sodium and potassium (two collections); morning urine volume and specific gravity (3 days); fasting haematocrit, serum osmolality, sodium, potassium, total protein, creatinine and urea (3 days); nude morning body mass (3 days); total body water by deuterium oxide dilution (days 1 and 3)
magnitude: Killer et al. (2014), coffee against water: 24-h urine volume 2409 ± 660 against 2428 ± 669 mL a day (abstract; ± unlabelled, read as SDs; equal to the means of the two collections by the editors' arithmetic; by collection 2593 against 2521 and 2226 against 2335 mL), difference −19 mL a day (editors' arithmetic); no interval, power calculation or within-person differences reported; editors' calculation treating the trials as independent (an upper bound on the width when a man's two trials are positively correlated): 95% CI about −290 to +250 mL a day (t, 49 df). Urine specific gravity 1.009 in all four collections; osmolality 217.7 and 243.7 against 208.2 and 202.1 mOsm/kg; urinary sodium 48.7 and 47.0 against 43.6 and 43.4 mmol/24 h (p = 0.02; editors' arithmetic: 3.6 to 5.1 mmol a day, about 8% to 12% higher). Total body water 51.5 ± 1.4 against 51.4 ± 1.3 kg (n = 25 by Figure 2; ± unlabelled, more likely standard errors by the editors' reading), condition p = 0.90, day p = 0.43. Body mass: no condition difference (p = 0.45); fall from day 1 to day 3 of 0.39 ± 0.5 kg across both trials (p<0.05), 190 ± 120 g a day by the Discussion (editors' calculation: about 0.5% of body weight). Morning urine volume p = 0.86, specific gravity p = 0.95. For scale, a 41% rise in 24-h urine reported after six cups following 5 days without caffeine (cited by the authors) would be about 1000 mL a day on these men's output (editors' arithmetic).

The abstract describes each trial as lasting three consecutive days. Funded by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), described as a non-profit organisation devoted to the study and disclosure of science related to coffee and health, stated to have had no role in design, analysis, the decision to publish or the manuscript; Killer and Blannin declared no competing interests, and Jeukendrup was employed by PepsiCo Inc. at the time of publication.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_killer_2014 (RoB 2, first pass): some concerns overall, in five of six domains. Random allocation to a counterbalanced order is stated, but sequence generation, concealment and the number in each sequence are not reported and period effects were not analysed; the setting was open-label and free-living, the 24-hour urine was collected by the men themselves, and adherence rests on booklets and a serum caffeine difference reported without values; total body water, the measure the authors call the gold standard, is shown for 25 of the 50 men with no reason given; there was no registration or prespecified primary outcome. The urine and blood measures are objective and reported for 42 to 50 men.

inconsistency.note: One study on file. The authors' own summary of earlier studies (second-hand) reports diuresis mainly with large amounts or after days without caffeine, and none at moderate amounts in people who habitually consume caffeine, which agrees with this result as worded.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for the trial's men, who habitually drank 3 to 6 cups a day, given instant coffee at the low end of their usual caffeine intake for 3 days; it says that women, people who rarely consume caffeine, larger amounts, other preparations and the hours after a cup were not studied.

imprecision.note: One study of 50 men reporting only non-significant p-values, with no interval, power calculation or within-person differences; the editors' conservative interval for daily urine (about −290 to +250 mL) excludes an excess as large as those reported after days without caffeine but not a small one, and total body water rests on 25 men with an unlabelled dispersion.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; no registration is mentioned.

grade.reasoning: Randomized crossover evidence starts high; down one level for risk of bias (unreported randomization details and period effects, open label with self-collected urine, total body water missing for half the men without explanation, no registration) and one for imprecision (a single study of 50 men reporting only non-significant p-values, without an interval or power calculation): low. Rated as worded: no detectable change in daily urine output and hydration markers over 3 days in men who habitually drank coffee, at about their usual caffeine intake, compared with the same volume of water. The claim does not say that coffee hydrates exactly as water does, because 'similar' was never tested against a margin: by the editors' conservative calculation a coffee excess of more than about 250 mL of urine a day is unlikely and a smaller one is not excluded. 'Does not detectably change' rather than 'insufficient evidence' because the data exclude an effect as large as those the authors cite after days without caffeine, though not a small one. Status single study. Funding by a coffee-science institute and one author's employment by a beverage company are reported as flags, not used to rate down (METHODS §1.4). The urinary sodium difference is reported because it is the study's one significant difference. Amounts appear only as the study conditions.

statement: In 369 adults aged 18 to 62 in Bristol, UK (analysed out of 416 randomized, as an earlier report of this study gives: Rogers et al., 2010), who had gone without caffeine from at least 7 PM the evening before (checked by salivary caffeine), caffeine capsules (study conditions: 100 mg at 11:15 AM and 150 mg at 12:45 PM) compared with identical placebo capsules, given double-blind and assigned at random (stratified by the intake people reported at their recruitment interview and by age; the two groups compared were set afterwards from a questionnaire on the week before testing, Rogers et al., 2010) in two groups, 212 'medium-high' consumers (40 mg of caffeine a day or more by that questionnaire; mean 235 mg) and 157 'non-low' consumers (less than 40 mg a day; mean 10.2 mg), is associated with the regular consumers returning to about the level of the low consumers given placebo, not rising above it in sleepiness, mental alertness or errors (their reaction times were numerically faster). In the afternoon tests (1:45 to 3:30 PM, after about 19 to 20.5 hours without caffeine for those on placebo, editors' arithmetic), regular consumers given placebo were the sleepiest, the least mentally alert (about 3.5 against 4.6 on a 0-to-8 self-rating, measured from a figure), the slowest on simple reaction time (485 against 437 ms) and the most error-prone (about 15.5 against 11.2 choice-reaction errors and 13.4 against 8.4 recognition-memory errors, measured from a figure). Given caffeine, they did not differ significantly from the low consumers given placebo in sleepiness, mental alertness (about 4.7), simple reaction time or errors (about 11.5 and 9.0), so caffeine made them no more accurate than the low consumers; their simple reaction time, 417 ms, was numerically faster than the low consumers' 437 ms, which the authors attribute to caffeine's motor effect. In the low consumers, caffeine reduced sleepiness and raised anxiety/jitteriness (about 0.7 against 1.65 on the 0-to-8 scale) without changing mental alertness or errors. Caffeine sped tapping by similar amounts in both groups (6.1 and 6.7 more taps in 30 seconds) and shortened reaction times in both; the authors summarize the result as faster but not smarter, and estimate that withdrawal slowed simple reaction time by 52 ms (their printed arithmetic gives 51), a large effect against an SD of 58 ms. The caffeine–placebo comparisons were randomized; the comparison between the consumer groups, which carries the 'undo withdrawal' reading, was not: people chose their own caffeine habits, the groups were compared after adjustment for sex, age and smoking only, and the authors note that knowing they had abstained could lower consumers' self-rated alertness and raise their sleepiness. At the 10:30 AM baseline, after the overnight break alone, the differences were small (simple reaction time 402 against 391 ms; choice-reaction errors 9.92 against 8.18). 'Smarter' was measured as errors on two simple computer tasks; results after the first capsule alone, the sizes and baselines of the placebo groups and intervals for any result are not reported. The authors report that other studies found no differences between consumer groups after overnight abstinence and that the withdrawal-reversal account has been widely disputed (not read here), while an older study found the same pattern. An earlier report of the same participants and testing (Rogers et al., 2010), counted here with the 2013 report as one study, not two, gives who was left out: of 416 randomized, 4 lacked genetic data, 20 were excluded on a saliva check before the first capsule, 8 dropped out after at least the first capsule and 5 lost data to equipment faults, leaving 379 (162 non-low, 217 medium-high). All 5 medium-high consumers who dropped out had been given placebo, 4 giving headache and feeling sick as their reasons, so the medium-high placebo group analysed may lack those most affected by abstinence; the 2013 analysis, which also needed complete task data, has 10 fewer people (5 in each group), not itemized in either report. Splitting each group at its median (mean intakes 1.3, 19, 128 and 346 mg a day), the 2010 report found that caffeine raised anxiety in the two lower-intake groups (about 1.25 against 0.51 and 1.37 against 0.75 on the 0-to-8 scale, measured from its Figure 1) but not in the two higher; that on placebo, self-rated alertness was lower the higher the habitual intake (about 4.92, 4.75, 4.38 and 3.74), while caffeine raised it only in the two higher-intake groups (to about 5.08 and 4.92); and that the heaviest consumers given placebo reported the most headache (about 1.78 against 0.87 on caffeine). Before any capsule, higher intake already went with lower alertness and more anxiety and headache. These ratings come from the same testing as the 2013 report, whose authors say the earlier alertness score did not separate sleepiness from mental alertness, so the agreement is not a replication. The 2010 abstract goes further than its tests: it concludes that caffeine only brings frequent consumers' alertness back to baseline, with no net benefit, but no test against nonconsumers given placebo is reported, and the alternative that frequent consumers are less alert to begin with is argued against, not tested; it reports more headache on placebo in medium-high consumers, seen in the heaviest group only; and its claim of tolerance to caffeine's anxiety effect even among carriers of the genotype linked to that effect rests on a non-significant caffeine–placebo difference among 35 medium-high consumers with the TT genotype (about 0.37 points), about as large as a significant rise in non-low consumers with other genotypes (about 0.35; measured from its Figure 4). Funded by the UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (one grant for both reports); the first author has received grants for caffeine research from GlaxoSmithKline (Rogers et al., 2013) and, as declared in 2010 for the previous 3 years, consulting fees from Unilever and research grants from Barry Callebaut, Cadbury, DSM, GSK and Unilever (Rogers et al., 2010). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a lab study in Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to go without caffeine overnight; chance then decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills. The study was written up in two papers, in 2010 and 2013. By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine and got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest, felt least alert and made the most mistakes. Caffeine brought them up to about the level of people who rarely have caffeine, with no fewer mistakes than them. In everyone, caffeine sped up finger tapping and reaction times. In people who rarely have caffeine it also raised anxiety and jitters, but not in people who often have it. All 5 people who often have caffeine and quit the test day early had been given dummy pills; 4 gave headache and feeling sick as their reasons. People chose their own caffeine habits, so the groups may differ in other ways, and the authors say other studies disagree.
population: 369 adults aged 18 to 62 in Bristol, UK: 157 'non-low' consumers (under 40 mg of caffeine a day by questionnaire, mean 10.2, SD 11.6; mean age 31.7; 85 women; 21 smokers) and 212 'medium-high' consumers (40 mg a day or more, mean 235, SD 146; mean age 33.8; 109 women; 41 smokers), non-smokers or light smokers (5 cigarettes a day or fewer), analysed only if salivary caffeine confirmed their consumer group and overnight abstinence and their data were complete; part of a larger protocol reported by Rogers et al. (2010) from the same participants and testing: 416 randomized (218 women, 198 men; 44% recruited from a postal survey in which only 10% took under 40 mg a day, so infrequent consumers were deliberately over-sampled: 162 of the 379 analysed there), with 4 left out for missing genetic data, 20 on a saliva check before the first capsule (15 non-low, 5 medium-high), 8 for dropping out after at least the first capsule (all 5 medium-high dropouts on placebo, 4 giving headache and feeling sick as their reasons) and 5 for equipment failures; the 369 here also needed complete task data, and the 10-person difference (5 per group) is not itemized in either report
exposure: Caffeine (anhydrous powder) in identical white capsules, 100 mg at 11:15 AM and 150 mg at 12:45 PM (study conditions, chosen by the authors to model afternoon caffeine levels after two to three cups of ground coffee earlier in the day), after abstinence from at least 7 PM the previous evening; random, double-blind assignment within each consumer group (77 low and 106 regular consumers given caffeine, Table 2), stratified by the intake reported at the recruitment interview and by age, the groups analysed being set afterwards from the questionnaire (Rogers et al., 2010)
comparator: Identical cornflour placebo capsules at the same times within each consumer group (80 and 106 by the editors' subtraction; not printed); for the 'withdrawal' reading, low consumers given placebo, a non-randomized benchmark that the authors treat as normal for the time of day

evidence.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory study at the University of Bristol, UK. Results are reported for 369 participants aged 18 to 62, non-smokers or light smokers (5 cigarettes a day or fewer; smoking not permitted during the test day until they left the laboratory), included only if salivary caffeine confirmed their consumer group and overnight abstinence and their data were complete. A questionnaire on the week before testing divided them into non-low consumers (less than 40 mg of caffeine a day; n = 157, mean 10.2 ± 11.6 mg, age 31.7 ± 12.1 years, 85 women, 21 smokers) and medium-high consumers (40 mg a day or more; n = 212, mean 235 ± 146 mg, age 33.8 ± 12.7 years, 109 women, 41 smokers). Within each group they were randomly assigned to caffeine (anhydrous powder; 100 mg at 11:15 AM and 150 mg at 12:45 PM) or cornflour placebo on both occasions, in identical white capsules given double-blind; the authors chose the doses to model afternoon caffeine levels after two to three cups of ground coffee earlier that day. Participants abstained from caffeine from at least 7:00 PM the previous evening, arrived at 9:30 AM and did an approximately 30-minute test battery four times: at 10:30 AM (baseline), 45 min after the first dose, and 60 and 135 min after the second dose. The regression analyses of those given caffeine include 77 non-low and 106 medium-high consumers (Table 2); the placebo-group sizes are not printed. Funded by a UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council grant (BBS/B/01855); the first author has received grants to support research on caffeine from GlaxoSmithKline. Editors' arithmetic: placebo groups 80 (157 − 77) and 106 (212 − 106); time without caffeine at least about 15.5 hours at the 10:30 AM baseline and at least about 18.75 to 20.5 hours at the afternoon tests (1:45 to 3:30 PM) for those given placebo.

evidence.extracted: The authors state that caffeine did not affect recognition-memory or choice-reaction errors in non-low consumers and did not improve medium-high consumers' performance above that of non-low consumers given placebo, so that, at least from these results, it would seem that caffeine fails to acutely enhance mental performance. Tapping was affected to the same extent in both groups and did not differ between the two placebo groups; caffeine increased mean tapping speed by 6.1 (non-low) and 6.7 (medium-high) taps per 30 s, which the authors read as a motor effect independent of habitual intake. Their summary: caffeine clearly enhances motor performance (faster tapping and reaction times in both groups) but does not appear to improve mental performance ('not smarter'), because medium-high consumers gain no net increase in mental alertness from their habit and, in non-low consumers, at least at the amounts given, reduced sleepiness is offset by more anxiety/jitteriness. evidence.extracted: The abstract concludes that tolerance to caffeine's effects on sleepiness means that frequent consumption fails to enhance mental alertness and mental performance; the Discussion states that the rise in mental alertness and performance after caffeine in medium-high consumers represents a return to the normal state (reversal of the adverse effects of withdrawal) rather than an enhancement above it. risk_of_bias.note: The answer rests on a non-randomized comparison: whether caffeine lifts regular consumers above normal or only back to it is judged against low consumers given placebo, and the two consumer groups chose their own habits and were compared after adjustment for sex, age and smoking only; the authors name self-selection and knowledge of abstinence (which could lower consumers' self-rated alertness and raise their sleepiness) as possible biases and answer self-selection with other studies, not with these data. By ROBINS-E standards this comparison is at high risk of bias from confounding (card sc_rogers_2013). The randomized caffeine–placebo contrast itself has some concerns (card sc_rogers_2013, RoB 2): sequence generation, concealment, placebo-group sizes, baseline values by arm and the numbers excluded are not reported, and only the runs after the second dose are shown in detail. The earlier report of the same testing (Rogers et al., 2010; card sc_rogers_2010) gives the numbers left out of its own analysis (416 randomized, 379 analysed) and adds two concerns: randomization was stratified on the intake reported at the recruitment interview and on age, while the groups analysed were set afterwards from a questionnaire, so stratification does not guarantee balance within them; and all five medium-high consumers who dropped out after a capsule had been given placebo, four giving headache and feeling sick as their reasons, so missing data in that placebo group probably depend on the outcome (which, if anything, makes its deficit look smaller). Neither report prints the placebo-group sizes.

inconsistency.note: One study on file, in two reports (Rogers et al., 2010, shares its participants and testing and cannot count as agreement; its Discussion makes the same misclassification argument against studies that found caffeine raised alertness in infrequent consumers). Its authors report that studies by other groups found no differences between consumer groups after overnight abstinence (Haskell et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2006) and that the withdrawal-reversal account has been widely disputed, while an older study found the same pattern as this one (Goldstein et al., 1969); none of these has been read, so the disagreement is rated second-hand: down one level, to be revisited when they are on file.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: the claim is worded for the conditions tested (two capsules after about 15.5 to 20.5 hours without caffeine, one afternoon, self-ratings and simple computer tasks) and says that 'smarter' meant errors on two simple tasks; it is not worded for everyday drinking, other amounts or complex thinking.

imprecision.note: Not rated down: 369 participants, 77 to 106 a group, and clear F tests for the main contrasts; no intervals are reported and the group means are shown only as bars, which the claim gives as approximate figure measurements.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; no registration is mentioned.

grade.reasoning: The caffeine–placebo contrast was randomized and double-blind, so the evidence starts high; down two levels for risk of bias, because the answer to the question (whether caffeine lifts regular consumers above normal or only back to it) rests on comparing them with self-selected low consumers, and one for inconsistency (other studies, as the authors describe them, disagree): very low, the floor. The randomized caffeine–placebo differences within each group alone would rate higher (high minus one level for unreported randomization details and selective presentation of time points: moderate). Rated as worded, an association: in this study, regular consumers given placebo did worse in the afternoon than low consumers given placebo, and caffeine brought them back to about that level without making them more accurate, while it sped tapping in both groups. Whether the deficit was caffeine withdrawal, as the authors conclude, and whether caffeine never gives regular consumers a net mental benefit, are the authors' interpretation, which one comparison of self-selected groups cannot establish; the claim says so. Rogers et al. (2010), now read, reports the same participants, testing, treatments, rating scales and grant (the 2013 report says it already reported part of these data, from the same cohort), so the two are counted as one study, not two (§6.3, overlapping evidence): its anxiety and alertness results by habitual intake agree with the 2013 report but do not replicate it, and the evidence base, the certainty and the status are unchanged. It adds who was randomized and left out (416 randomized; all five medium-high consumers who dropped out were on placebo, most giving headache and feeling sick as reasons) and that randomization was stratified on the intake reported at recruitment, both recorded under risk of bias without a further downgrade (the rating is already at the floor, and the dropouts would, if anything, make the deficit look smaller). Its abstract goes beyond its tests (no test against nonconsumers given placebo; more headache on placebo in the heaviest consumers only; tolerance in genetically susceptible people inferred from a non-significant result in a small subgroup); the claim gives these conclusions as the authors' interpretation. Status single study. Doses appear only as the study conditions.

statement: In adults studied mostly in general-population cohort studies, with case-control and cross-sectional studies in some analyses and short randomized trials for blood pressure, lipids and one pregnancy trial, pooled in 201 published meta-analyses of observational studies (67 outcomes) and 17 of randomized trials (9 outcomes) up to July 2017 and re-analysed in an umbrella review (Poole et al., 2017, corrected in 2018; no specific funding), drinking coffee compared with drinking none or less is associated with lower risks of death and of several diseases, and with higher risks of some pregnancy outcomes and of fracture in women. All-cause death: in the most recent dose–response meta-analysis the relative risk was lowest at about three cups a day compared with none, 0.83 (95% confidence interval 0.79 to 0.88, as corrected in 2018; misprinted as 0.83 to 0.88 in both the abstract and the Results); it was 0.90 (0.85 to 0.96) at seven cups a day and 0.96 (0.94 to 0.97) per extra cup a day in a linear analysis, and the association was consistent across all earlier meta-analyses. Cardiovascular death was lowest at about three cups a day (0.81, 0.72 to 0.90); high compared with low intake went with less incident cancer (0.82, 0.74 to 0.89) and type 2 diabetes (0.70, 0.65 to 0.75), and the largest associations were with liver disease (chronic liver disease 0.35, 0.22 to 0.56; liver cancer 0.50, 0.43 to 0.58). The review gives no absolute risks. In pregnancy the associations went the other way: high compared with low intake went with low birth weight (odds ratio 1.31, 1.03 to 1.67; 2 cohort studies), pregnancy loss (1.46, 1.06 to 1.99; 5 cohort studies, I² 87%) and preterm birth in the first (1.22, 1.00 to 1.49) and second trimester (1.12, 1.02 to 1.22), each from a single meta-analysis and, by the authors' account, from subgroup analyses of articles on total caffeine; the one randomized trial in pregnancy (1153 participants) found no significant difference in preterm birth (0.81, 0.48 to 1.37). Fracture was not associated with coffee overall, but high intake went with more fractures in women (1.14, 1.05 to 1.24) and fewer in men (0.76, 0.62 to 0.94), in studies many of which did not adjust for body weight, smoking, calcium, vitamin D or alcohol. A higher risk of lung cancer with coffee was not seen in people who had never smoked (0.92, 0.75 to 1.10); the authors judge it likely that residual confounding by smoking can explain the apparent higher risk. The authors rated the quality of evidence for about 75% of outcomes as very low and 25% as low (GRADE), and report that Mendelian randomization studies, which use gene variants linked to coffee drinking, found no genetic evidence that coffee lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes or of all-cause and cardiovascular death, suggesting that residual confounding could explain those associations, while noting that the method assumes a straight-line relation (these studies have not been read here, and the review's eligibility criteria excluded studies of genetic polymorphisms for coffee metabolism). Because smoking, age, body weight and alcohol go with coffee drinking, coffee may mark higher income or education, and people may cut down on coffee when early illness begins (all named by the authors), these associations cannot show that coffee causes any of them; the three-cup level is where observational dose–response curves were lowest, not an amount tested in people. A correction published in 2018 (BMJ 2018;360:k194) fixed eight numerical errors, among them two other results at three cups a day printed with the estimate outside its interval: decaffeinated coffee and all-cause death, 0.89 (0.85 to 0.93), printed as 0.83 (0.85 to 0.89), and stroke death, 0.70 (0.57 to 0.86), printed with 0.80 to 0.90. The authors state that the errors do not affect their findings; one corrected estimate, liver cirrhosis with any coffee against none (0.89, 0.73 to 1.08), is no longer statistically significant. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A large review pulled together earlier reviews of research on coffee and health, mostly studies that followed people for years. People who drank coffee died a bit less often during these studies than people who drank none, and had lower rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease. In pregnancy the links went the other way: more coffee went with low birth weight, preterm birth and losing the pregnancy; women who drank more had more fractures, while men had fewer. A link with lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked. Because these studies only watched people, they cannot show that coffee is the reason, and studies of genes found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying. The review's authors rated most of this evidence very weak, and they later corrected a few numbers that had been printed wrong.
population: Adults in the studies pooled by published meta-analyses up to July 2017: mostly general-population cohort studies (only one included meta-analysis concerned people with established disease, two small cohorts after myocardial infarction), with case-control and cross-sectional studies in some meta-analyses and short randomized trials for blood pressure, lipids and one pregnancy trial; pregnant women for the pregnancy outcomes
exposure: Coffee drinking, mostly self-reported cups a day (cup size and strength not standardized), compared as high against low (or no) consumption, any against none, one extra cup a day, or along non-linear dose–response curves; decaffeinated coffee separately
comparator: Low or no coffee drinking; in randomized trials, no coffee
outcome: All-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality; incident cardiovascular disease, cancers, type 2 diabetes, liver, neurological and other diseases; pregnancy outcomes; fracture; in randomized trials, blood pressure, lipids and birth outcomes
magnitude: Poole et al. (2017, corrected in 2018), relative risks (odds ratios where the source meta-analysis used them) with 95% CIs, no absolute risks: all-cause mortality 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88) at three cups a day against none, 0.90 (0.85 to 0.96) at seven cups, 0.96 (0.94 to 0.97) per extra cup; cardiovascular mortality 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90) at three cups; incident cardiovascular disease 0.85 (0.80 to 0.90); incident cancer 0.82 (0.74 to 0.89) high against low; type 2 diabetes 0.70 (0.65 to 0.75) high against low, 0.94 (0.93 to 0.95) per cup; chronic liver disease 0.35 (0.22 to 0.56) and liver cancer 0.50 (0.43 to 0.58) high against low. Pregnancy, high against low: low birth weight OR 1.31 (1.03 to 1.67), pregnancy loss 1.46 (1.06 to 1.99; I² 87%), preterm birth first trimester 1.22 (1.00 to 1.49), second trimester 1.12 (1.02 to 1.22); randomized trial, preterm birth 0.81 (0.48 to 1.37). Fracture, high against low: women 1.14 (1.05 to 1.24), men 0.76 (0.62 to 0.94); per cup women 1.05 (1.02 to 1.07), men 0.91 (0.87 to 0.95). Lung cancer in people who never smoked, any against none, 0.92 (0.75 to 1.10). Authors' GRADE: about 75% of outcomes very low, 25% low. Corrected in 2018 (BMJ 2018;360:k194), with the values first printed: all-cause mortality at three cups 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88), printed with 0.83 to 0.88; decaffeinated coffee and all-cause mortality at three cups 0.89 (0.85 to 0.93), printed as 0.83 (0.85 to 0.89), and 0.90 (0.79 to 1.01) at the highest intake; stroke mortality at three cups 0.70 (0.57 to 0.86), printed with 0.80 to 0.90; liver cirrhosis, any against none, 0.89 (0.73 to 1.08), printed as 0.61 (0.45 to 0.84). The authors state that the errors do not affect their findings.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_poole_2017 (AMSTAR 2, first pass): critically low confidence in the umbrella review (no protocol, no list of excluded articles, an unexplained language restriction); the included meta-analyses were taken as published without checking the primary studies, many pooled odds, rate and hazard ratios together, and eight numerical errors had to be corrected in 2018. In the primary cohorts, coffee drinking goes with smoking, age, body weight and alcohol and may mark income or education, people may cut down on coffee when illness begins, and many fracture studies were not adjusted for body weight, smoking, calcium, vitamin D or alcohol; these could change the size of the associations, not only their meaning.

inconsistency.note: About 40% of the 83 re-analysed meta-analyses had significant heterogeneity, 90% of these with I² above 50% (pregnancy loss 87%), and the authors list differences in populations, coffee types, exposure measures, follow-up and outcome assessment without resolving them. The mortality association was consistent in direction across meta-analyses, and the opposite fracture associations in women and men are reported as a subgroup finding, not counted as inconsistency.

indirectness.note: Not rated down: worded as associations in the populations studied, mostly general-population cohorts with self-reported cups of varying size and strength, and pregnant women for the pregnancy outcomes.

imprecision.note: Not rated down separately: most intervals for the main associations exclude no association by a clear margin (all-cause death 0.83, 0.79 to 0.88, at three cups as corrected in 2018; 0.90, 0.85 to 0.96, at seven cups; 0.96, 0.94 to 0.97, per cup), but the first-trimester preterm-birth interval reaches 1.00 and low birth weight rests on 2 cohort studies; the claim states these limits.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down separately: Egger's test could be run on 40% of the re-analyses and showed small-study effects in 20% of those (for example type 2 diabetes and hip fracture); none is reported for the mortality estimates, and the authors say unmeasured publication bias may affect many estimates.

large_effect.note: Only the high-against-low associations with liver cancer and chronic liver disease reach the size that can allow an upgrade, and reverse causation and other habits of coffee drinkers could inflate them; not applied.

dose_response.note: The mortality curves are non-linear, with the lowest risk at about three cups a day rather than a steady gradient; not applied.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (an umbrella review of critically low confidence that took meta-analyses as published, with confounding and reverse causation in the primary cohorts) and one for inconsistency (substantial unexplained heterogeneity across many outcomes): very low, the floor, in line with the authors' own GRADE for most outcomes (about 75% very low, 25% low; the rating for each outcome is in an appendix not read). Rated as worded, an association: people who drank coffee had somewhat lower relative risks of death and of several diseases, and higher risks of some pregnancy outcomes and, in women, of fracture. Whether coffee causes any of these is a separate question that these designs cannot answer, and the Mendelian randomization studies the review cites found no genetic evidence that coffee lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes or of all-cause and cardiovascular death; they are reported as the review describes them and have not been read. The three-cup level is where dose–response curves in observational data reached their lowest point, not an amount tested in people, and it is not presented as guidance; no amounts are given in the plain lines. The three misprinted results are given as corrected in 2018 (BMJ 2018;360:k194, now read with the article); the correction fixed eight numerical errors that the authors state do not affect their findings, which holds for the direction of the associations used here, though the corrected estimate for liver cirrhosis with any coffee against none is no longer significant. No absolute risks are given, so none are stated. Status replicated: the review reports the mortality association as consistent across all earlier meta-analyses, which share cohorts and count once, and describes two later, independent cohorts in Europe and North America with the same direction; this agreement does not raise the certainty. The question was reworded from 'Is coffee good or bad for your health?' because the evidence shows associations, not effects.
